# Overview

In this final lab, you will bring together the skills developed throughout the course by creating interactive dashboards with Shiny. 
You will first build a dashboard using a dataset used in Labs 4 and 5 to learn the structure and functionality of a Shiny application. 
You will then create a dashboard using the dataset you have worked with throughout the course. 
The goal of this lab is to transform static analyses into interactive tools that allow users to explore data, visualize patterns, and support decision-making.
By the end of this lab, you will have created two functional dashboards that integrates data, visualizations, maps, and user controls into a single analytical product.

Part 1: Building a Dashboard with the Instructor Dataset

Using the dataset provided by your instructor, create a Shiny dashboard that includes the following components.

Required Features
User Input

Include at least two interactive controls:

selectInput()
sliderInput()
checkboxInput()

You may choose any two that are appropriate for the data.

Visualization

Include at least one interactive visualization that changes based on user selections.

Examples:

Bar chart
Line chart
Scatterplot
Histogram
Data Table

Include a table that updates based on user inputs.

Dynamic Summary

Include at least one summary statistic or text output that changes when the user interacts with the dashboard.

Examples:

Number of incidents
Average value
Percent change
Most common category
Reflection Questions
What user inputs did you include and why?
How does the dashboard improve data exploration compared to a static visualization?
What challenges did you encounter when building the application?
Part 2: Creating a Dashboard Using Your Course Dataset

Using the dataset you selected earlier in the course, build an interactive dashboard that allows users to explore your data.

This dashboard should incorporate visualizations and maps developed during Labs 4 and 5.

Required Components
Dashboard Layout

Use an organized layout such as:

sidebarLayout()
tabsetPanel()
Multiple panels or sections
User Controls

Include at least three user inputs that allow users to filter or explore the data.

Examples:

Date range
Category selection
Geographic area
Incident type
Numeric threshold
Visualizations

Include at least two visualizations developed from your earlier work.

Examples:

Trend chart
Distribution plot
Comparison chart
Faceted visualization
Map

Include at least one map developed from Lab 5.

Examples:

Point map
Choropleth map
Density map
Summary Statistics

Include dynamic summaries that update based on user selections.

Examples:

Total incidents
Average values
Counts by category
Percent changes
Analytical Narrative

Include a brief written section within the dashboard or in your submission that addresses:

What analytical question does the dashboard help answer?
What patterns or findings are most important?
Who is the intended audience?
How could the dashboard support decision-making?
Submission Requirements

Submit the following:

Shiny application files (app.R or equivalent)
A rendered HTML document describing the dashboard
Screenshots of the completed dashboard
Responses to all reflection questions

# How to Submit

Download the [template for this lab](../labs/templates/lab-05-LastName.zip?raw=true) prior to beginning the lab. 

<br>

### Knitting to HTML

When you have completed your assignment, click the "Knit" button to render your `.RMD` file into a `.HTML` report.

<br>

### Special Instructions

Upload both your `.RMD` and `.HTML` files to the appropriate link for this assignment on the Canvas page for this course.

<br>

### Before You Submit

Remember to ensure the following before submitting your assignment.

  * Name your files using this format: **Lab-##-LastName.rmd** and **Lab-##-LastName.html**
  * Show both the solution for your code and write out your answers in the body text 

See [Google's R Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/Rguide.xml) for examples of common conventions.

<br>
<br>

### Common Knitting Issues

`.RMD` files are knit into `.HTML` and other formats procedural, or line-by-line.

* An error in code when knitting will halt the process; error messages will tell you the specific line with the error
* Certain functions, like `install.packages()` or `setwd()`, are bound to cause errors in knitting 
* Altering a dataset or variable in one chunk will affect its use in all later chunks
* If an object is "not found", make sure it was created or loaded with `library()` in a previous chunk

**If All Else Fails:** If you cannot determine and fix the errors in a code chunk that's preventing you from knitting your document, add `eval = FALSE` inside the brackets of `{r}` at the beginning of a chunk to ensure that R does not attempt to evaluate it, that is: `{r eval = FALSE}`. This will prevent an erroneous chunk of code from halting the knitting process.
